extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents/attorneys, and patent examiners (Canada) (also PCT applicants/practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards used by Canadian patent examiners and practitioners for assessing patent applications (patentability, amendments, disclosure, unity, claim drafting) including intersections with PCT practice and case law precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new subject-matter in amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Any amendment must not introduce new subject-matter such as to contravene section 38.2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments to Canadian (non‑PCT) applications must meet the requirements of section 91 of the Patent Rules and comply with all of section 38.2 of the Patent Act (with noted exceptions). PCT national phase applications are governed by different provisions (section 155.7 and related references to 155.6) and certain subsections of 38.2 do not apply to PCT national phase entries; equivalents and exceptions are described (see paragraphs 261–262). In all cases hypothetical additions must not introduce subject‑matter outside the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness implies requirement for ingenuity (non‑obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement codified in section 28.3 of the Patent Act that an invention not be obvious in view of certain prior art implies a requirement for ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is supported by multiple cases (e.g., Janssen‑Ortho v. Novopharm; Canamould; Baker Petrolite; Harvard College; Diversified Products) and underlies the substantive non‑obviousness/inventive step inquiry under Canadian law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing/Pozzoli approach to assessing obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach based on Windsurfing International v. Tabur Marine and refined in Pozzoli SPA v. BDMO SA (the Windsurfing/Pozzoli approach) is adopted as the framework for obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach (as cited in Apotex Inc. v. Sanofi‑Synthelabo Canada Inc.) provides a stepwise analytical framework used by courts and examiners when assessing obviousness. The manual references the approach and related jurisprudence for application in Canadian cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited and fact‑sensitive applicability of the 'obvious‑to‑try' test
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'obvious‑to‑try' test has been applied in some contexts (e.g., downhole drilling equipment) but its appropriateness is fact‑sensitive and subject to appellate comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wenzel Downhole Tools applied the obvious‑to‑try test to downhole drilling equipment; the FCA later commented on the appropriateness of that test on appeal. Examiners should apply obvious‑to‑try cautiously and in context, with attention to appellate guidance (see paragraphs 199–200).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enabling disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent specification must provide sufficient disclosure enabling a person skilled in the art to practice the invention; Minerals Separation and Consolboard articulate the requirements of sufficient disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minerals Separation (and its endorsement in Consolboard) remains a primary statement of the sufficient disclosure standard. The manual repeatedly cites these cases to indicate the expectations for the content and quality of the description so that the invention can be performed by the skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity — avoidably obscure or ambiguous language renders a patent invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is invalid if it relies on 'language which, when fairly read, is avoidably obscure or ambiguous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle appears in Natural Colour Kinematograph and related case law. Examiners should ensure claims and specifications are clear and not avoidably obscure; ambiguous language will be viewed in the context of the whole specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity / single invention requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one patent may issue for a given invention; a patent shall be granted for one invention only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolboard and Teva confirm the one‑invention rule. If multiple inventions are disclosed, applicants may file divisional(s) — either one divisional to cover several additional inventions or multiple divisionals each covering one of several inventions disclosed in the parent application (see paragraph 264).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of chemical and mathematical formulae in applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical and mathematical formulae are permissible in patent applications as provided by subsection 51(2) of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection 51(2) expressly governs the permissibility; the practice manual also indicates permissibility of such presentation in applications is implied from subsection 51(2). Examiners should accept formulae presented in accordance with the Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product produced by a method may be obvious (double‑patenting/double protection risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method for preparing a product would usually be considered to render the product it produces obvious, potentially creating an appearance of double‑patenting if claims to product and method appear in different applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting and examining claims, consider the relationship between method and product claims to avoid double‑patenting issues. The manual warns of the usual treatment that method steps leading to a product can make the product claim obvious in light of the method claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound prediction of utility requires a factual basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual basis is required to support a sound prediction of an advantage (utility), including when asserting an advantage for a selection from a broader group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eli Lilly and related cases require that any factual basis needed to support a sound prediction of an advantage possessed by a selected compound or selection from a broader group must be present in the disclosure (see paragraph 257 and cited cases). Examiners should look for supporting facts and data in the specification when applicants rely on sound prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject‑matter for computer‑implemented inventions: technological solution requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a computer‑implemented invention must provide a technological solution to a technological problem (i.e., provide a technological solution to a technological problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual uses this formulation when discussing mental steps and computer‑implemented subject matter (see paragraph 285). Examiners should assess whether claimed subject matter delivers a technological contribution rather than merely abstract or mental steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals — definition of 'propagating' for signal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A signal is considered to be propagating even if it is moving in a closed loop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office Practice Regarding Signals (C.P.O.R. Vol. 135, No. 33, Aug 14, 2007) clarifies propagation for signal claims; examiners should treat signals that circulate in closed loops as propagating for claim interpretation (see paragraph 296).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence listings and free‑text sequence data: follow WIPO ST.26 guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Free text and language‑dependent free text in sequence listings should follow the PCT sequence listing standard, WIPO Standard 26 (ST.26); see paragraphs 85–88 of that standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More information and examples are found in the PCT ST.26 and the manual cross‑references those sections (see paragraph 260). Examiners and filers should conform to ST.26 for sequence listings and related free‑text fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adoptive definitions and field‑specific terminology (e.g., 'analyte', stem cell types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are adopted from authoritative sources (e.g., 'analyte' defined broadly; stem cell definitions from NIH glossaries) for interpretive clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual adopts definitions (see paragraphs 301–316) and uses concrete examples to illustrate when a measure or sample source is 'standard' or 'non‑standard' to the person skilled in the art (e.g., measuring analyte X in saliva vs urine, or timing of post‑exposure testing). Examiners should apply these adopted definitions when interpreting specifications and prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay with U.S. practice and MPEP for publication and patentability interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Information regarding U.S. patent document publication and certain interpretation issues is provided by reference to U.S. practice as expressed in the USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual cites MPEP sections (e.g., on 101 and 103) as interpretive aids for issues such as publication and patentability in some contexts (see paragraph 118). While Canadian law governs, U.S. practice can inform certain procedural or interpretive matters where referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright protection of source code not a patentability criterion but relevant IP consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Source code for computer programs may be subject to protection under the Copyright Act as a literary work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While copyright protection does not determine patentability, the manual notes the availability of copyright for source code (see paragraph 283), which is relevant for applicants and examiners when considering the full IP landscape around software‑related inventions.
